It was the front axle and steering wheel of a rusted-out 1974 Sears Roebuck lawnmower that must have washed off the sound side during a hurricane years back. And tangled right around the rusted steering column was Earl's old lead-head jig. Earl walked over, unhooked his lure, and told Luther he was wondering where he left his grass-cutter.

There was a fellow over in Duplin County by the name of Luther Higgins who swore up and down he could tell his livestock blindfolded by the sound of their chewing. Cecil Boney, his neighbor down the road, wouldn't have given you a plugged nickel for Luther's hearing, especially after Luther’s prize Chester White boar spent three straight nights turning Cecil’s prize butterbeans into a plowed field.

Cecil caught the beast red-handed, scooped it into the back of his old Dodge truck, and drove right over to Luther’s porch. Cecil told him flat out that either Luther paid for the butterbeans or the hog was going to spend the night locked in the county pound. Luther looked that pig right in the eye, spat out his tobacco, and said that wasn't his hog at all because his hog had a crooked tail, whereas that brute’s tail had a decent curl to it.

They argued back and forth for an hour over the geometry of pig tails until the sun went down. Finally, Cecil got fed up, hauled the hog down to the sheriff's office in Kenansville, and dumped it on the steps just to spite them both.

Come to find out next morning, neither one of 'em owned the animal. It had busted out of a livestock trailer three weeks prior down near Wallace, and had been working its way north, eating high on the hog at five different farms while letting everybody in the township fight over who had to feed it next.

runs.reply: Now, about twenty miles this side of Boone, back before the parkway was ever paved, there stood an old water mill that belonged to a man named Luther Vance. Luther was a quiet sort who kept to himself, mostly because he spent all his time trying to outsmart a six-pound rainbow trout that lived right under the mill wheel. Every evening after the stones stopped turning, Luther would walk out on that slick timber with his fly rod, and every evening that trout would just rise up, flick its tail, and sink back down like it was thumbing its nose at him. Luther tried every fly in his book—coachmen, woolly buggers, royal Wulffs—and the fish wouldn't so much as look at 'em. Well, word got around the county, as things do, and folks started coming down to the creek just to watch Luther get beat by a fish. One Saturday in July, a slick-talking fellow from Raleigh drove up in a shiny blue Chevrolet, wearing store-bought waders and carrying a rod that looked like it cost more than Luther's truck. He walked right up to Luther and laid down a twenty-dollar bill on the stump. "I'll take that trout on the first cast," the fellow said, loud enough for half the county to hear. Luther looked at the twenty, then looked at the water, and slow as molasses, he folded the bill up and put it in his shirt pocket. "Go on then," Luther said. "He's all yours." The man waded right out into the middle of the tailrace, hauled back that fancy rod, and let fly. The line whistled through the air and landed right on a dime. But the second that fly touched the water, the mill wheel gave a sudden, heavy clunk—someone had opened the sluice gate up top. The current surged, the line tangled in a clump of water willow, and before the man could blink, his expensive rod was jerked right out of his hand and went spinning down the creek. The crowd on the bank let out a holler. But Luther didn't laugh. He just reached down into his bait can, pulled out a squirming red wiggler—not a fly in sight—and dropped it over the side of the timbers. That six-pound trout came straight up, took the worm without a ripple, and stayed right there on the end of the line. Luther pulled him in, unhooked him gentle, and dropped him back into the deep pool. The fellow from Raleigh stood dripping wet on the bank, looking at his empty hands. "I thought you were a fly fisherman," he said. Luther wiped his hands on his overalls and smiled just a little bit. "I am," he said. "The fish just has his own opinions on the matter."

There was a fellow over in Duplin County named Earl Oates who fancied himself the sharpest trader this side of the Cape Fear River. Earl went down to the livestock barn in Kenansville and bought himself a big old gray mule named Roscoe that the seller swore could plow straight furrows all day on half a bucket of sweet feed and a kind word.

Well, Earl hitched Roscoe up Monday morning, took a fresh grip on the reins, and hollered for the mule to walk. Roscoe just planted his four hooves in the red clay, lowered his long ears, and went to sleep right there in the middle of the turn row. Earl yelled, he switched, he cussed until the crows flew out of the pecan trees, and Roscoe didn't twitch so much as a fly off his flank.

By noon, Earl was red in the face and ready to trade the brute for a sack of turnips when the steam whistle at the peanut mill blew twelve o'clock. The second that whistle shrieked, Roscoe threw his head up, trotted three miles of straight rows without a break, and stopped dead at the fence line the very second the whistle died away.

Earl figured he had himself a schedule-bound animal, so the next morning he brought a tin horn out to the field and blew it himself to get a head start. Roscoe opened one lazy eye, gave Earl a look that plain said he wasn't fooled for a nickel, and went right back to sleep. Earl ended up having to pay the night watchman at the mill five dollars a week to blow the steam whistle whenever Earl felt like breaking ground.
